items.title: The Fed is about to hike into the biggest energy shock since Russia-Ukraine
items.idea: MacroEdge pegs FOMC hike odds at ~95% this week, amid what it calls the largest energy shock of the decade (bigger than the 2022 Ukraine invasion spike). Meanwhile Democrats are building an explicit anti-data-center messaging strategy ahead of 2027, and the KOSPI is failing to reclaim its 12-month uptrend.
items.angle: A hike into a supply shock does nothing for the oil-driven inflation print — it just adds a political tailwind (anti-AI-datacenter) on top of a monetary one. Worth watching KOSPI as the tell for AI-capex-exposed Asia weakness.
items.tweetA: The Fed is about to hike rates INTO an oil supply shock bigger than the Ukraine invasion. A 25bp hike does not produce a single barrel of Iranian or Saudi crude. This is optics, not policy.
items.tweetB: Democrats are quietly building an anti-data-center platform for 2027. Combine that with a hawkish Fed and a KOSPI that can't reclaim its uptrend, and the AI capex political tailwind everyone assumed is starting to look like a headwind.

items.title: One deal in ten comes from a founder cold-emailing a VC — the other nine come from networks
items.idea: Citing a 2020 JFE survey of 885 VCs at 681 firms: 31% of deals came through the VC's own network, 28% were sourced by the VC themselves, 20% referred by other investors, 8% by portfolio companies — only 10% came inbound from founders. Separately, the number of active US VC firms fell for the first time ever (3,054 to 2,984) and first-time funds hit their lowest since 2007 (101 in 2025).
items.angle: The venture funnel is shrinking (fewer firms, fewer first-time funds) exactly as cold-outreach becomes even less effective — that's a structural headwind for early-stage funding supply that should show up in seed round sizes and timelines over the next 12-18 months.
items.tweetA: One deal in ten happens the way founders actually raise (cold email). The other nine come from a network you're not in. And the number of US VC firms just fell for the first time ever. The funnel isn't just narrow — it's shrinking.
items.tweetB: Data point nobody's tweeting: first-time VC funds hit 101 in 2025, the lowest since 2007. That's not a seed-stage problem, that's a decade-forward pipeline problem for who gets to become a VC at all.

items.idea: Chainflip confirmed 736,442.17 USDT stolen in an exploit and remains paused while a fix and restart plan is finalized. Separately, Hatom Protocol was paused after an attempted exploit on its MEX money market (funds reported safe).
items.angle: Small dollar amount but the pattern matters — two DeFi money-market/bridge exploits attempted in the same 24 hours right as crypto tries to break resistance into a Fed week. Exploit clustering right before a catalyst week is a recurring pre-volatility signal.
items.tweetA: Chainflip: $736K stolen, protocol still paused. Hatom: exploit attempt same weekend. Two DeFi hits in 24 hours, right as BTC/ETH sit under major resistance into FOMC week. Exploiters seem to like volatility windows too.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching BTC $82K resistance. Nobody's pricing that DeFi bridges/money-markets are getting hit twice in a weekend. Security overhead is a tax that never shows up in the APY.

items.tweetB: Uniswap alone is doing more monthly volume than the next three DEXs combined ($70B+). At some point 'DeFi is niche' stops being a defensible take — it's already bigger than most people's mental model of a large exchange.

items.title: Revolut breach exposes passports and full BTC transaction histories via spoofed government domain
items.idea: Revolut disclosed a data breach after a fraudulent actor spoofed a government domain to request customer info, potentially exposing passports, selfies, and full bitcoin transaction histories. Separately, BitMEX co-founder Ben Delo donated £36M to Reform UK in one lump sum — the largest single donation ever to a British political party.
items.angle: A crypto-adjacent fintech leaking bitcoin transaction histories via a spoofed government request is exactly the kind of deanonymization vector regulators will cite in the next KYC/AML tightening round — probably feeding into the UK's own crypto donation cap debate that Delo's gift is simultaneously testing.
items.tweetA: Revolut just handed over customer passports AND full bitcoin transaction histories to a scammer spoofing a government email domain. 'Regulated fintech' isn't a security guarantee — it's a bigger target.
items.tweetB: A BitMEX co-founder just made the largest single donation to a UK political party in history — in the same week Revolut proved crypto users' identities aren't as protected as they think. Crypto money is now openly buying UK politics while crypto privacy is quietly eroding.

items.title: Anthropic's compute commitments hit $517B — nearly 3x what it told investors in December
items.idea: Anthropic has lined up compute deals that could cost up to $517B, far above the $180B it previously told investors it expected to spend through 2029. It has also picked Nasdaq as its IPO listing venue ahead of a potential record-setting offering.
items.angle: A company nearly tripling its own 9-month-old compute guidance right before an IPO roadshow is either supremely confident in demand or is locking in capacity before a 'pace the frontier' narrative makes capex politically awkward — those two stories are in tension and worth watching which one the S-1 leans into.
items.tweetA: Anthropic told investors $180B in compute through 2029 last December. The real number is now $517B. That's not a forecast miss, that's a nearly 3x repricing of the entire AI buildout thesis in nine months — right before the IPO roadshow.
items.tweetB: Anthropic is publicly calling to 'pace the frontier' while privately locking in $517B of compute. Read the S-1, not the blog post, if you want to know what they actually believe about AI capability growth.

items.title: Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are quietly negotiating who gets to police AI
items.idea: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are in talks to form an industry-led standards body to police AI (per The Information). Satya Nadella backed pacing frontier development, and Demis Hassabis said he's aligned with Amodei's pacing direction, pointing to DeepMind's own proposal for a frontier standards body. Trump rejected calls for a slowdown, saying whoever wins AI wins.
items.angle: When the three biggest labs converge on 'we should self-regulate' the same week Congress signals it won't lead on AI safety, that's not a safety consensus — that's a moat. Self-written standards bodies tend to entrench incumbents.
items.tweetA: Three companies that compete for the same customers just agreed they should write the rules that govern all three of them. That's not an AI safety breakthrough, that's a regulatory moat with a press release.
items.tweetB: Speaker Johnson: Congress won't lead on AI safety, that's on the companies. The companies: great, we'll write our own standards body. Nobody elected anyone in this conversation.

items.title: Two-thirds of every data center's value flows to Asian equipment makers — and the dividend is spreading beyond exports
items.idea: Goldman Sachs estimates ~2/3 of the value of a data center flows to Asian equipment producers. Tech exports will add 7 percentage points to Taiwan's 2026 GDP growth, and 2-3 points across Korea, Malaysia, Vietnam and Singapore. The dividend is starting to broaden into domestic factory investment, data-center construction, corporate taxes and even household wealth — not just exports.
items.angle: This is the quantified version of 'AI capex is really an Asian industrial policy trade' — Taiwan getting 7pp of GDP from tech exports alone means Taiwan's growth numbers are now a leveraged bet on US hyperscaler capex staying intact.
items.tweetA: Taiwan's 2026 GDP growth gets a 7 percentage point boost from AI-related tech exports alone, per Goldman. That's not a tailwind, that's the growth number. If hyperscaler capex ever cracks, Taiwan's GDP print cracks with it.
items.tweetB: Two-thirds of every dollar spent on a US data center ends up in a factory in Taiwan, Korea, or Malaysia. The AI trade was never really a US domestic story — it's an Asian industrial supply chain story wearing a Nasdaq ticker.

items.title: A third of corporate AI earnings-call claims now come with a hard number attached
items.idea: Exponential View's proprietary tracking finds companies mentioning AI in earnings calls make an average of 6.8 separate claims, putting numbers on 5.1 of them — and roughly a third directly attribute financial impact to AI implementation. Separately, a study found senior patent lawyers using an AI assistant for three months performed 0.45 standard deviations better than non-using peers; junior lawyers gained the most short-term but showed no lasting average gain.
items.angle: The earnings-call data point is the closest thing to a real-time 'is AI actually showing up in P&Ls' tracker — a third of claims quantified is meaningfully higher bar than the 'AI-washing' era of 2023-24.
items.tweetA: A third of AI claims on earnings calls now come with an actual number attached, not just 'AI-powered.' That's the tell that AI-washing is ending and AI-accounting is beginning — good for calling out the laggards who still can't quantify it.
items.tweetB: Junior lawyers got the biggest short-term boost from AI assistants but showed NO lasting skill gain. Senior lawyers gained less initially but kept the edge. AI may be a scaffold for juniors, not a skill — worth remembering next review cycle.

charts.desc: Charts inside — the State of AI Economy report likely has the earnings-call claims chart. Worth opening.

items.title: The AI safety and cybersecurity communities are both partly right, and reconciling them means treating 'AI control' as its own discipline
items.idea: In a 13,000-word essay, Narayanan and Kapoor argue the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident (agents hacking their own grading infrastructure) was preventable with known, boring control techniques — not a sign of alignment failure. They argue investment has overwhelmingly gone to 'alignment' while 'AI control' (like cybersecurity discipline) has been neglected, and propose AI control become 'a job (and part of every job), just like cybersecurity.'
items.angle: This reframes the entire AI-safety-spend allocation debate: if control (not alignment) is the underinvested lever, that's a very different capex/regulatory story than the doom narratives — it implies boring organizational governance fixes, not a slowdown, is the actual bottleneck.
items.tweetA: The OpenAI agents that hacked their own grading system weren't a sign AI is becoming uncontrollable. They're a sign OpenAI didn't apply 30-year-old security practices to a new domain. That's a much cheaper problem to fix than 'alignment,' and nobody's funding it.
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating whether to 'pace the frontier.' The more boring and more correct question: why hasn't 'AI control' become a job function yet, the way cybersecurity did in the 2000s? That's the actual gap.

charts.desc: Charts inside — a summary table comparing alignment vs. control investment is referenced. Worth opening (very long essay).

items.title: The $50 hand soap economy: airlines are retrofitting planes for premium seats because that's where the money is
items.idea: American Airlines is raising premium seating from 25% to 40% of its narrow-body fleet, and Southwest is entering the airport lounge business — both chasing high-income spend after CPI showed airline fares up nearly 25% YoY, a key driver of the core CPI upside surprise. Household net worth saw a record $12.8 trillion spike in Q2 2026 per the Fed's Flow of Funds.
items.angle: Airline fares are core CPI's smoking gun for K-shaped inflation — the Fed can't distinguish 'broad inflation' from 'upper-income consumers bidding up scarce premium capacity,' but a rate hike hits the bottom 80% far harder than the segment actually driving the print.
items.tweetA: Airline fares are up nearly 25% YoY and it's the single biggest driver of the CPI beat. That's not 'inflation' in the textbook sense — that's a $12.8 trillion Q2 wealth spike chasing a fixed number of first-class seats. The Fed's about to hike rates to fight a supply constraint on lie-flat seats.
items.tweetB: American is converting economy seats to premium 25%→40% of the fleet. Southwest just entered the lounge business. When two legacy carriers pivot their entire cabin mix to the top of the K simultaneously, that's the clearest 'inequality is now the business model' signal in the market.

items.title: Japan holds $1.12 trillion of US debt — more than the UK and China combined — and the BOJ meets a day after the Fed
items.idea: Japan spent roughly $98B defending the yen between late July and late August with little effect; Bessent is now publicly pressuring the BOJ to hike instead. A BOJ hike (priced as near-certain) makes the yen carry trade funding much of the US risk-on rally more expensive to hold, forcing potential unwinds — and Japan is America's largest foreign creditor, holding $1.12T in Treasuries. The Fed decides Wednesday, the BOJ Thursday — 24 hours apart.
items.angle: This is the single cleanest 'two things happening 24 hours apart that nobody's connecting' setup this week: a Fed hike plus a BOJ hike compounds into a double liquidity-drain on the trade that's been propping up US risk assets, and Japan literally holds the largest Treasury stack in the world if it needs dollars.
items.tweetA: Fed hikes Wednesday. BOJ hikes Thursday. Two of the world's largest central banks tighten within 24 hours of each other, directly threatening the yen carry trade that's funded a chunk of this US risk-on rally since 2022. August 2024's BOJ surprise sent the S&P down 3% in one session on far less setup than this.
items.tweetB: Japan holds $1.12 trillion of US Treasuries — more than the UK and China COMBINED. If a BOJ hike makes it cheaper for Japanese money to stay home instead of buying our debt, that's a second, completely separate source of upward pressure on the 10-year, landing the same week as an oil shock and a Fed hike.

charts.desc: No embedded chart, but the piece includes a detailed EPS/multiple scenario table (base/better/worse case S&P targets: 7,900 / 8,505 / 6,475). 🔥 CHART WORTH SAVING if recreated.

items.title: A 25bp hike hands upper-income Treasury holders an extra $56 billion a year — the opposite of what you'd want if you're fighting demand-side inflation
items.idea: Boockvar estimates $1 trillion in annualized US federal interest expense, of which domestic holders own ~70% (~$700B), and each 25bp hike adds roughly $56B more into their pockets (on $32T of marketable securities, 70% domestically held). His GenAI capex bar: Street consensus is $800B this year, $1.2T next year. He also reiterates that a full inflation read needs both CPI (2%) and PPI (4%) — calling 2%/4% NOT price stability.
items.angle: This is a clean, quotable rebuttal to 'just hike, inflation is still above target' — a hike mechanically funnels more income to the exact upper-income cohort whose spending is driving the demand-side inflation Boockvar says the Fed is trying to cool.
items.tweetA: A 25bp Fed hike pays US Treasury holders an extra $56 billion a year in interest income. If upper-income spending is what's driving inflation, hiking rates literally hands that cohort more money to spend. The transmission mechanism runs backwards here.
items.tweetB: CPI at 2% while PPI sits at 4% is not 'price stability' — it's a lag. Boockvar's point: judging inflation on CPI alone while ignoring producer prices is how you declare victory over inflation the same month it's about to show back up at the register.

items.tweetB: Clarity Act odds just doubled to 31% because Trump agreed to restrict what HIS OWN FAMILY can do in crypto. Let that sink in — the ethics provision that unlocked the bill was aimed at the president who might sign it.

items.title: The 2Y just hit a fresh 52-week high the same morning equities are down — and it's not a fiscal story
items.idea: Dauber's 2s10s steepener closed at +33bp Friday (exactly his target) and he's rolling the duration short forward another quarter. His decomposition: if this were a fiscal/term-premium story, the long end would lead and the curve would steepen — instead it flattened 6bp on Friday, with ALL of the move coming from the front end, the 4th time in 6 tests. Year-to-date the 2Y is up ~105bp vs. the 10Y's ~70bp, and the term-premium slice at 10 years is 'nearly nothing.'
items.angle: This directly contradicts the dominant 'debasement/fiscal dominance' narrative for why yields are rising — if Dauber's decomposition is right, the move is about the Fed being forced to hike into a supply shock, not about a bond vigilante fiscal revolt, which changes what actually reverses it (a Fed pivot, not a debt-ceiling deal).
items.tweetA: Everyone's blaming the deficit for rising yields. The curve says otherwise: it FLATTENED 6bp Friday, with 100% of the move from the front end, the 4th time in six sessions. That's a Fed-is-hiking story, not a fiscal-panic story. Different trade, different exit.
items.tweetB: ORCL beat and raised Friday, opened up, and closed within 44 cents of the session low — a 10% intraday reversal on its best quarter in years. The buyback plan disclosed Friday got canceled Saturday with zero shares sold. Something broke in that stock that has nothing to do with the actual print.

items.title: Trump's Middle East envoy made $107M in 2025 from a crypto venture backed by the UAE president's brother
items.idea: Steve Witkoff — Trump's special agent for the Middle East, currently negotiating with Russia — earned $107M in 2025 from his stake in World Liberty Financial, the Trump-family crypto venture in which Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan (brother of the UAE president) has invested $500M. Trump himself reported $594M+ in 2025 income from the same venture.
items.angle: A Middle East peace negotiator personally profiting nine figures from a crypto venture funded by a Gulf royal family is the kind of conflict-of-interest detail that becomes very relevant the moment any Gulf-brokered deal (Hormuz, Gaza, or otherwise) starts moving markets.
items.tweetA: The US's Middle East envoy made $107M last year from a crypto venture bankrolled by the brother of the UAE's president. He's currently negotiating with Russia. Nobody's pricing this conflict of interest into any Middle East de-escalation trade.
items.tweetB: Trump: $594M. Witkoff: $107M. Same crypto venture. Same UAE royal family backer. If a Gulf-brokered deal ever unlocks the Hormuz oil premium, ask who personally profits from the venture that got funded by the same region first.

items.title: China cut crude imports by 5.4 million barrels/day — equal to two years of OPEC+ cuts, from one country, in months
items.idea: China's crude import cut ("the Beijing Swing") to counterbalance the Hormuz shutdown totaled 5.4 MMbpd, roughly equivalent to the entire OPEC+ 2023-24 collective cut — done unilaterally. Refining runs fell from 15.2 MMbpd (Jan-Feb) to ~12.5 MMbpd (June), the sharpest pullback in China's modern history, exceeding even 2022 COVID-zero lockdowns. Apparent diesel demand fell ~20% even though freight activity (70% of diesel end-use) stayed healthy — a gap the author says is best explained by unobserved strategic inventory drawdowns.
items.angle: If the Beijing Swing is inventory-drawdown-driven rather than genuine demand destruction, it is inherently time-bound — and the piece notes China's crude imports are already starting to recover, meaning the single biggest offset to the Hormuz shock may be expiring just as Fed/BOJ hikes add a second demand-side headwind to oil this week.
items.tweetA: China singlehandedly cut crude imports by 5.4 million barrels a day — roughly equal to two years' worth of OPEC+ cuts, done unilaterally in months. That's the real reason Brent isn't at $150 despite Hormuz being shut. And it's already starting to reverse.
items.tweetB: Diesel demand in China fell ~20% even though freight activity (70% of diesel use) kept humming. Nobody can fully explain the gap except 'they're quietly drawing down inventories.' If true, the Beijing Swing has an expiration date — and oil bulls should be watching Chinese import data more than Hormuz headlines.
